[ The studio ]

Fragment Foundry is a four-person generative-graphics studio in Berlin. We make real-time visual systems — title sequences, installation backdrops, generative brand marks, and the occasional album cover — all rendered live on the GPU. We work in raw WebGL because we like to understand every instruction that touches a pixel.

How a fragment shader actually works

A page builder thinks in boxes. A GPU thinks in pixels — millions of them, all coloured at once. To draw the shaders on this site we hand the graphics card two tiny programs and one flat shape, then let it run the second program independently for every pixel on screen. Here is the whole pipeline:

1 · Geometry

We upload one full-screen triangle — three corners that cover the whole canvas. That's the only shape involved.

2 · Vertex shader

Runs once per corner. It just places those three points in clip space — our version is four lines long and never changes.

3 · Rasterizer

The GPU fills the triangle, figuring out which screen pixels it covers — typically every pixel on the canvas.

4 · Fragment shader

Runs once per pixel, in parallel. Given the pixel's coordinate, our GLSL returns its colour. This is where all the art lives.

5 · Pixels

The results land in the framebuffer and the browser shows them. Sixty times a second, the whole thing repeats.

Uniforms: the dials we turn

A fragment shader is the same code for every pixel, so on its own it can only draw something static. Uniforms are values that stay constant across all pixels for a single frame but can change between frames — they're how we feed the shader the outside world. Every shader on this site receives three:

u_time makes a formula move; u_resolution lets it adapt to any canvas size; and u_mouse lets the cursor reach in and bend the image. Each gallery piece also declares its own custom uniforms — u_speed, u_zoom, u_segments — and those are exactly what the stage sliders write to, live, with no recompile.

Why this is impossible in a page builder

Tools like Gutenberg compose pre-made blocks of HTML. There is no block for "run a C-like program on the graphics card and paint the result every frame." The work happens below the document — in GLSL, compiled by the GPU driver at runtime. We surface compile errors, manage context loss, cap the pixel ratio for performance, and respect prefers-reduced-motion by freezing to a still frame. None of that is content; all of it is code.
